extracted.intended_audience: ML/AI researchers, dataset authors, HCI researchers, educators, and practitioners interested in dataset documentation and ethics
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating ethical sensitivity in ML engineers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and measurement framework for observing how ML engineers notice and reason about ethical issues in unfamiliar training data, using think-aloud sessions, funnel-sequence interviews, and analysis of recognition, particularization, and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (first mention of an ethical issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first time a participant mentioned a particular ethical issue. The study recorded the time the utterance started, the relevant comment text, and the screen contents shown when the recognition occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count an instance as recognition only if participants outwardly expressed concern, even if vague. Examples: describing facial recognition as 'scary' is counted as recognition; mentioning a dataset that had been in the news without voicing objection is not counted. Record whether recognition was unprompted (during think-aloud) or prompted (during interview). Note ambiguity: recognition may be gradual (not a single awakening), so time-to-first-recognition may not be a meaningful measure in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularization
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined (quote) as: 'Seeking information, reflecting, and making developmental evaluations about the situation, stakeholders, consequences, responsibility, options, resources, and the relationship of the issue to the task.' While coding, label these utterances as 'particularization' and record the time, context notes, and screen contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record which options participants considered, constraints they mentioned, examples or stories they offered, comments about signals of credibility in sources they referred to, and comments that signaled understanding of technical and social aspects (how it happens and its impacts). If participants cite remembered information, record the information's source and topic. Particularization often reveals differences in social and technical understanding and is well captured by think-aloud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment (consideration of a course of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Label a statement as a judgment if a participant considered a course of action (e.g., used phrases like 'I would' or 'we should'). Judgment captures the participant's proposed interventions or choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish judgment from particularization (which may list options without committing). Record time and context; note that judgment is less frequent in short think-aloud sessions. Track common judgments (e.g., put a human in the loop, replace dataset, alter demographic distribution) and note when participants revise judgments after reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funnel-sequence time categories (Time A / B / C) for recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Three time categories used to classify recognition in funnel-sequence interviews: Time A (participant describes perception), Time B (participants asked about moral aspects without direct ethics question), Time C (directly asked about ethics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map observation moments to Time A/B/C: compare first recognition during think-aloud to Time A, interview questions 1-6 to Time B, and direct ethics question (Question 7) to Time C. Record whether first recognition occurred in A/B/C to capture prompted vs unprompted recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think-aloud session protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Protocol for eliciting ethical sensitivity: 25-minute think-aloud where participants explore dataset/problem statement/Datasheet (as assigned), decide 'whether and how' to use the data while thinking aloud; screen and audio are recorded; participants are not interrupted and stop after ~25 minutes, followed by a funnel-sequence interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants can view data in Google Drive or download it. Randomly assign participants to conditions (e.g., Datasheet vs no Datasheet). Obtain consent for audio/screen recording; be prepared for occasional recording failures. Allow participants to conclude early. Follow the think-aloud with a funnel interview (summary/clarifying questions, indirect moral questions, then direct ethics question).

rubrics_metrics.name: Datasheet engagement and design guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics and guidance about Datasheet use: whether participants opened/read the Datasheet, how extensively they relied on it during particularization, and whether it prompted (unprompted) recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track whether participants opened the Datasheet and how much they read; 10/11 in study opened it. Note that long documents may overwhelm readers—authors should consider making Datasheets brief, offering an outline or linked navigation, or highlighting key sections. Datasheet content that triggers recognition includes information about data distribution, provenance, curation, sampling/selection, testing, and modifications to the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcription, coding, and annotation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure for generating analyzable data: use automated transcription (e.g., otter.ai), correct transcripts by listening to audio, and then read transcripts while watching screen recordings to label verbalizations (recognition, particularization, judgment) and collect timings and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative analysis software (e.g., NVivo 12) to label utterances and record start times. Also record times each document was opened and navigated away from during the session. Label whether ethical verbalizations in the interview were 'prompted' or 'unprompted.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and interpreting cues for recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: What to consider as cues when identifying recognition: participants often read snippets aloud, highlighted text, pointed with their mouse, or paraphrased study materials; when none of these occur, researchers may infer screen content but not precise gaze.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask participants follow-up (but many struggle to describe what 'tipped them off'); try reworded prompts ('What tipped you off?') but expect limited reliability. Use combined transcript and screen-recording evidence to infer cues; be cautious interpreting ambiguous utterances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of ethical issue types
rubrics_metrics.description: A taxonomy of ethical issues to record and count during analysis: discrimination from demographically unrepresentative training data; high stakes in facial recognition (false positives); privacy and consent in provided training data; privacy/consent in data collected from deployment (store); other privacy concerns; unconscious bias in law enforcement/security; justice implications of predictive policing ('Pre-Crime').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count and report occurrences/frequencies of these issue categories (the study enumerated counts). Use these categories to analyze which datasource or prompt led to recognition and how participants particularized each issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome and intervention evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures and suggestions for evaluating interventions (context documents, curricula, policies) intended to foster ethical sensitivity: track recognition rates, particularization depth/duration, prevalence and quality of judgments, and behavioral outcomes (e.g., deciding to replace dataset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For curricula: support recognition by teaching common cues and relevant ethical issues; support particularization by training source evaluation, risk assessment, and socio-technical reasoning; support judgment by practicing decision-making in case studies. For organizational interventions: consider prompts in meetings or forms, intermittent prompts, independent advice channels, and embedding ethical engagement into job descriptions and performance reviews. Use think-aloud + funnel interview framework to measure intervention effects.
